title: Volumes of Elementary Solids and Solids of Revolution

items.title: A solid between continuous graphs over a compact Jordan base
Solids of revolution about a coordinate axis
The product of a content-zero set and a compact interval has content zero
items.strategy: Given a finite rectangle cover of the bounded content-zero set with total base volume below an assigned tolerance, take products with the interval. Product volumes multiply by the interval length, so choosing the base tolerance relative to that length gives the required cover. Treat the empty set, a degenerate interval, and zero length before dividing by any length.

items.title: The graph of a continuous function on a compact Euclidean set has content zero
items.strategy: Place the compact domain in a fixed bounding cube and use uniform continuity. Partition the cube into small coordinate cells. Above every cell meeting the domain, the graph lies in a vertical stack whose height is the oscillation of the function plus two mesh widths. The number of base cells times their base volume stays bounded by the bounding-cube volume, so the total covering volume tends to zero with the modulus of continuity and the mesh. This extends the published rectangle-domain theorem without assuming that the compact domain is Jordan measurable.

items.title: The boundary of a solid between continuous graphs over a compact Jordan base has content zero
items.strategy: Bound both graph functions on the compact base. Show that the boundary of the solid is contained in the two graphs together with the product of the base boundary and one bounding vertical interval. The two graphs have content zero by the compact-domain graph theorem; the base boundary has content zero by the Jordan boundary criterion, so its product with the interval is null by the product lemma. A finite union and every subset of a null set are null.

items.title: A solid between continuous graphs over a compact Jordan base is Jordan measurable and integrates by vertical sections
items.strategy: The defining inequalities make the solid closed, and compactness of the base plus boundedness of the graph functions makes it bounded; Heine--Borel therefore gives compactness. The boundary lemma and the Jordan boundary criterion give Jordan measurability. A continuous integrand is integrable on that compact Jordan set, every vertical section is the interval between the two graph values, and Jordan--Fubini gives the displayed iterated formula. Explicitly allow coincident graphs, an empty base, and degenerate vertical sections.

items.title: The volume under a nonnegative continuous graph over a compact Jordan base is its integral
items.strategy: In the solid theorem take the lower graph to be zero, the upper graph to be the nonnegative function, and the integrand to be one. The inner integral is the height of the section. Include the empty base and the identically-zero graph.

items.title: The disc formula for the volume of a solid of revolution
items.strategy: For a nonnegative continuous profile on a compact interval, first view the planar region between its positive and negative graphs as a compact Jordan base. The rotated solid is the region between the two continuous square-root graphs over that base, so the general solid theorem makes it compact Jordan. Its section perpendicular to the axis is a closed disc of radius equal to the profile value. Cavalieri and the published Jordan disc-area formula give the sectional area $\pi f(x)^2$ and hence the volume formula.

items.title: The washer formula for a solid of revolution between two nonnegative profiles
items.strategy: For continuous $0\le g\le f$, each axial section is the closed disc of radius $f(x)$ with the open disc of radius $g(x)$ removed. Its Jordan content is $\pi(f(x)^2-g(x)^2)$ because the shared boundary circle has content zero. Establish compact Jordan measurability from the same square-root graph construction as the disc theorem, then apply Cavalieri. Treat $f=g$, $g=0$, and both coordinate-axis orientations.

items.title: A right circular cylinder of radius $R$ and height $h$ has volume $\pi R^2h$
items.strategy: Apply the disc formula to the constant profile $R$ on an interval of length $h$. Separate $R=0$ or $h=0$ before the positive-parameter computation.

items.title: A right circular cone of radius $R$ and height $h$ has volume $\pi R^2h/3$
items.strategy: For $h>0$, apply the disc formula to the linear profile $f(x)=Rx/h$ on $[0,h]$ and evaluate the resulting quadratic integral from its polynomial primitive. Handle $R=0$ separately and do not divide by a zero height.

items.title: A closed three-dimensional ball of radius $r\ge0$ has volume $4\pi r^3/3$
items.strategy: For $r>0$, regard the ball as the solid of revolution with profile $\sqrt{r^2-x^2}$ on $[-r,r]$. The disc formula reduces its volume to $\pi\int_{-r}^r(r^2-x^2)\,dx$, and the fundamental theorem gives $4\pi r^3/3$. At $r=0$ the ball is a singleton and has content zero.

items.title: The volume of a three-ball by Cavalieri's cylinder-minus-cones proof
items.strategy: State the same $4\pi r^3/3$ conclusion as the disc proof but use a genuinely different route. At every height $z\in[-r,r]$, the ball section has area $\pi(r^2-z^2)$ by the Jordan disc formula. The section of a radius-$r$, height-$2r$ cylinder after removing the two cones with common vertex at the centre has the same area. Finite additivity computes the comparison solid from the proved cylinder and cone volumes, and Cavalieri equates it with the ball. Handle $r=0$ and cross-reference the disc proof only in an authored Remark, not as a logical dependency.

items.title: The cylindrical-shell formula for a solid of revolution about the $y$-axis
items.strategy: Let $0\le a\le b$ and let the nonnegative profile be continuous on $[a,b]$. View the rotated solid as the region under the radial height function over the compact annulus; the main solid theorem gives Jordan measurability and volume as an integral over that annulus. Separate $a=b$ before using nondegenerate partitions. For $a<b$, use finite Jordan-cover bounds on radial subannuli, whose contents are differences of disc contents. Uniform continuity makes the upper-minus-lower sum tend to zero, while either tagged sum differs negligibly from the Riemann sum for $2\pi x f(x)$. Include $a=0$ and zeros of $f$.

items.title: Closed Euclidean balls are Jordan measurable and their volumes satisfy the slicing recursion
items.strategy: For $n=1$ the radius-$r$ ball is $[-r,r]$ and has content $2r$. Induct on $n$. The $n$-ball is the solid between the graphs $\pm\sqrt{r^2-\|u\|_2^2}$ over the $(n-1)$-ball, so the main theorem gives compactness and Jordan measurability. Slicing instead by the last coordinate, the section at $t$ is an $(n-1)$-ball of radius $\sqrt{r^2-t^2}$. Apply the published determinant-scaling theorem to the scalar dilation of the unit $(n-1)$-ball, then Cavalieri, to obtain $V_n(r)=V_{n-1}(1)\int_{-r}^{r}(r^2-t^2)^{(n-1)/2}\,dt$. Treat $r=0$, $n=1$, endpoints $t=\pm r$, and the zero-radius sections.

title: Volumes of Elementary Solids and Solids of Revolution: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A radius-$2$, height-$3$ cylinder and cone have volumes $12\pi$ and $4\pi$
items.strategy: Substitute $R=2$ and $h=3$ into the proved cylinder and cone formulas and check that the cone occupies one third of the corresponding cylinder volume.

items.title: A torus with major radius $R$ and minor radius $r$ has volume $2\pi^2Rr^2$
items.strategy: Assume $R>r>0$ and rotate the disc $(x-R)^2+y^2\le r^2$ about the $y$-axis. At height $y$, the outer and inner radii are $R\pm\sqrt{r^2-y^2}$, so the washer area is $4\pi R\sqrt{r^2-y^2}$. Integrate from $-r$ to $r$ and use the established disc-area integral to obtain $2\pi^2Rr^2$. Verify that $R>r$ prevents the inner radius from changing sign.

items.title: The shell and washer methods both give $8\pi/3$ for a rotated parabolic cap
items.strategy: Use the source region $0\le x\le2$, $(x-1)^2\le y\le1$, revolved about the $y$-axis. The shell formula gives $2\pi\int_0^2x(1-(x-1)^2)\,dx=8\pi/3$. Horizontal washers have radii $1\pm\sqrt y$ and give $\int_0^1 4\pi\sqrt y\,dy=8\pi/3$. Evaluate both proper integrals and compare.

items.title: Gabriel's horn has finite improper volume $\pi$
items.strategy: For each $R>1$, apply the disc formula to the profile $f(x)=1/x$ on $[1,R]$, obtaining $\pi\int_1^R x^{-2}\,dx=\pi(1-1/R)$. Let $R$ tend to infinity using the definition of an improper integral. State only the finite-volume half here; the infinite lateral-surface conclusion belongs to `regular-surfaces-and-surface-integrals`, where the surface-area formula is developed.

items.title: Slicing gives the unit-ball volumes through dimension five
items.strategy: Start from $V_1(1)=2$ and apply the slicing recursion successively. Evaluate the required integrals of $(1-t^2)^{1/2}$, $1-t^2$, $(1-t^2)^{3/2}$, and $(1-t^2)^2$ by the disc-area formula, elementary polynomial primitives, and the Wallis-integral recurrence. Obtain $2,\pi,4\pi/3,\pi^2/2,8\pi^2/15$ without using the later Gamma closed form.

items.title: A compact subset of $\mathbb R^3$ need not be Jordan measurable
items.strategy: Let $S$ be the Smith--Volterra--Cantor set and take $E=S\times[0,1]^2$. It is closed and bounded, hence compact, and has empty interior, so it equals its boundary. For any finite box cover, partition the last two coordinates at every box endpoint. At an interior point of each resulting planar cell, the active boxes project to an interval cover of $S$ and therefore have total first-coordinate width at least $1/2$. Multiply by the cell area and sum to obtain a positive lower bound for the covering volume. Thus the boundary is not content zero and $E$ is not Jordan measurable.

items.title: FALSE: every compact subset of $\mathbb R^3$ has Jordan volume
items.strategy: Invoke the preceding Smith--Volterra--Cantor product. It is a compact subset of three-space and is not Jordan measurable, so Jordan volume is undefined for this set.

items.title: FALSE: solids with equal parallel cross-sectional areas are congruent
items.strategy: Compare the boxes $[0,1]^3$ and $[0,2]\times[0,1/2]\times[0,1]$. Every horizontal section has area one, so Cavalieri gives equal volume. Their diameters are respectively $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt{21}/2$, which are unequal; Euclidean congruences preserve distances and hence diameter. Thus equal sections determine volume, not shape.

items.title: FALSE: one existing iterated integral guarantees multiple Riemann integrability
items.strategy: Use the published rational-versus-irrational section counterexample. Every integral in the first order exists and equals zero, but the lower and upper section-integral envelopes in the reverse direction have different integrals, so the bounded function is not multiply Riemann integrable.

title: The Real Gamma and Beta Functions

items.title: Log-convex positive functions
The real Gamma function by Euler's integral
Euler's Gamma integral converges exactly for positive real parameters
items.strategy: Split the integral at one. Near zero, real-power primitives handle $s\ne0$, while at the threshold $s=0$ the logarithmic primitive and the unbounded range of $\log$ give divergence; the exponential factor stays between positive constants. At infinity, choose a natural power dominating $t^{s-1}$ and use that the exponential dominates every polynomial. This proves convergence exactly for $s>0$ and discharges the Gamma definition's well-definedness.

items.title: Euler's real Beta integral
Euler's Beta integral converges exactly for two positive parameters
items.strategy: Split at $1/2$. Near zero the factor $(1-t)^{q-1}$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, so convergence is that of $t^{p-1}$; near one use $u=1-t$ and the symmetric comparison. Real-power primitives handle nonzero exponents, while the logarithmic primitive handles the threshold cases $p=0$ and $q=0$. Lower comparisons then give convergence exactly when $p,q>0$ and divergence at either forbidden endpoint.

items.title: The real Gamma functional equation $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$
items.strategy: For $s>0$, integrate by parts on $[\varepsilon,R]$. The boundary term tends to zero at both ends, using positivity of $s$ at zero and exponential domination at infinity. Pass to the improper limits separately and compute $\Gamma(1)=1$ directly.

items.title: $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$ for every natural number $n$
items.strategy: Use $\Gamma(1)=1$ for $n=0$ and induct with the functional equation. Keep the factorial recursion and zero index explicit.

items.title: The real Gamma function is smooth and its derivatives are logarithmic moments
items.strategy: On a compact parameter interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, dominate $|\log t|^kt^{s-1}e^{-t}$ separately near zero and infinity. At zero substitute $u=-\log t$; at infinity combine an integer-power bound with exponential decay. Repeated dominated differentiation gives $\Gamma^{(k)}(s)=\int_0^\infty(\log t)^kt^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$, including $k=0$.

items.title: The real Gamma function is strictly log-convex
items.strategy: For every $c>0$, write $c^s\Gamma(s)$ as an improper integral whose integrand is a positive exponential-affine function of $s$; strict convexity of the exponential and integration make this function strictly convex. Given two parameters, choose $c$ so the endpoint values agree. Convexity at their weighted point rearranges to strict log-convexity of Gamma.

items.title: The real Gamma function has one minimum and diverges at both ends of its domain
items.strategy: The recurrence gives $s\Gamma(s)=\Gamma(s+1)\to1$ as $s\downarrow0$. Strict convexity of $\log\Gamma$ and $\Gamma(1)=\Gamma(2)=1$ make its derivative cross zero exactly once in $(1,2)$, yielding one global minimum. Factorial values plus eventual increase give $\Gamma(s)\to\infty$ and $\Gamma(s)/s\to\infty$ at infinity.

items.title: Gautschi's inequality for the real Gamma function
items.strategy: For $x>0$ and $0\le s\le1$, apply log-convexity to $x+s$ between $x$ and $x+1$, then to $x+1$ between $x+s$ and $x+s+1$. Use the recurrence to obtain $x^{1-s}\le\Gamma(x+1)/\Gamma(x+s)\le(x+1)^{1-s}$. Check $s=0,1$ as equalities.

items.title: Log-convex solutions of the Gamma recurrence obey the Bohr--Mollerup factorial squeeze
items.strategy: For a positive normalized log-convex solution $f$ and $0<x\le1$, compare secant slopes at $n-1,n,n+x,n+1$. The recurrence evaluates integer values and expands $f(n+x)$ as a finite product times $f(x)$. Exponentiating gives factorial-product bounds whose ratio is $(n+x)/n$. Include $x=1$ and the first legal $n$.

items.title: Bohr--Mollerup characterisation of the real Gamma function
items.strategy: Gamma has the required positivity, normalization, recurrence, and log-convexity. Conversely apply the factorial squeeze to a candidate and to Gamma. On $0<x\le1$ both lie between common bounds whose quotient tends to one, so squeezing gives equality; the recurrence extends it to every positive real. Prove both directions.

items.title: Symmetry and the trigonometric form of the real Beta integral
items.strategy: The substitution $u=1-t$ gives symmetry. The substitution $t=\sin^2\theta$, first on compact interior truncations and then at both singular endpoints, gives $B(p,q)=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2p-1}\theta\cos^{2q-1}\theta\,d\theta$.

items.title: The real Beta--Gamma identity
items.strategy: Rectangular exhaustion and proper Fubini identify $\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)$ with the nonnegative improper first-quadrant integral. On compact truncations use $x=rt$, $y=r(1-t)$, whose absolute Jacobian is $r$. Exhaustion independence passes to $(0,\infty)\times(0,1)$, where Fubini factors the result as $\Gamma(p+q)B(p,q)$. Positivity permits division.

items.title: The elementary recurrences for the real Beta function
items.strategy: Insert the Gamma recurrence into the Beta--Gamma identity to obtain the two one-step recurrences, then add them to get $B(p,q)=B(p+1,q)+B(p,q+1)$. All denominators are positive.

items.title: $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ from the Gaussian integral
items.strategy: Substitute $t=u^2$ in Euler's integral to obtain $2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du$. Evenness makes this the full Gaussian integral, which is $\sqrt\pi$.

items.title: $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ by Wallis's product
items.strategy: The recurrence gives $\Gamma(n+1/2)=((2n)!/(4^nn!))\Gamma(1/2)$. Gautschi shows $\sqrt n\,\Gamma(n+1/2)/n!\to1$, while the published Wallis consequence gives $\sqrt{\pi n}\binom{2n}{n}/4^n\to1$. Comparing the positive limits yields the half-value. Cross-reference the independent Gaussian proof.

items.title: Stirling's factorial asymptotic holds up to a positive constant
items.strategy: Compare $\log r$ with the integral of $\log t$ over $[r-1/2,r+1/2]$. The series for $\log(1+u)$ bounds the symmetric error by a constant multiple of $1/r^2$, so the error series converges. Summing and evaluating the logarithmic integral makes $\log(n!)-((n+1/2)\log n-n)$ converge. Exponentiation gives $n!\sim C\sqrt n(n/e)^n$ for some $C>0$.

items.title: Wallis's product determines the Stirling constant as $\sqrt{2\pi}$
items.strategy: Insert the up-to-constant formula into $(2n)!/(n!)^2$, giving $\binom{2n}{n}\sim(\sqrt2/C)4^n/\sqrt n$. Compare with the Wallis asymptotic $4^n/\sqrt{\pi n}$ to get $C=\sqrt{2\pi}$.

items.title: Stirling's formula for factorials
items.strategy: Combine the undetermined-constant lemma with the Wallis identification. State the ratio form for positive integers and exclude $n=0$ from its square-root denominator.

items.title: The closed form for the volume of the unit $n$-ball
items.strategy: Induct from $V_1(1)=2$. In the slicing recursion substitute $u=t^2$ to identify the integral with $B(1/2,(n+1)/2)$. The Beta--Gamma identity and $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ cancel the induction factor and yield $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$.

items.title: The volume of a radius-$r$ closed $n$-ball is $\pi^{n/2}r^n/\Gamma(n/2+1)$
items.strategy: Use induction in the slicing recursion and $t=ru$ to prove $V_n(r)=r^nV_n(1)$ for $r>0$, then insert the unit formula. At $r=0$ both sides are zero.

items.title: The volume of the unit $n$-ball tends to zero with dimension
items.strategy: The closed form and Gamma recurrence give $V_{n+2}(1)/V_n(1)=2\pi/(n+2)$. Each parity subsequence is eventually bounded by a geometric sequence with ratio at most $1/2$, so both tend to zero and hence so does their interleaving.

items.title: The unit-ball volume is maximal in dimension five
items.strategy: Use $V_{n+2}/V_n=2\pi/(n+2)$ to locate the maxima of the even and odd subsequences at six and five. The finite-remainder Gregory--Leibniz formula gives $3<\pi<16/5$ from explicit odd and even partial sums. Evaluate $V_5$ and $V_6$; the upper bound gives $V_5>V_6$, so dimension five is the unique global maximum.

title: The Real Gamma and Beta Functions: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Special values of the real Gamma and Beta functions
items.strategy: Use normalization, the Gamma recurrence, the half-value, and the Beta--Gamma identity to compute $\Gamma(1)=1$, $\Gamma(2)=1$, $\Gamma(3)=2$, $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$, $\Gamma(3/2)=\sqrt\pi/2$, $B(1,1)=1$, and $B(2,3)=1/12$.

items.title: The unit-ball volumes through dimension eight from the Gamma formula
items.strategy: Substitute $n=1,\ldots,8$ into the closed form and use the Gamma recurrence and half-value to obtain $2,\pi,4\pi/3,\pi^2/2,8\pi^2/15,\pi^3/6,16\pi^3/105,\pi^4/24$.

items.title: A positive convex function need not be log-convex
items.strategy: On $(0,\infty)$ the identity is positive and affine, hence convex. Its logarithm is not convex: at the midpoint of $1$ and $4$, $\log(5/2)>\log2=(\log1+\log4)/2$. This is the possible converse to the design's impossible request for a log-convex function that is not convex.

items.title: A positive non-log-convex solution of the Gamma functional equation
items.strategy: Put $D=	frac12(\log\Gamma(1)+\log\Gamma(3/2))-\log\Gamma(5/4)$ and $A=1+|D|$, and define $F(s)=\Gamma(s)e^{A\sin(2\pi s)}$. Periodicity gives $F(s+1)=sF(s)$ and $F(1)=1$, while $F(5/4)\ne\Gamma(5/4)$. At the midpoint $5/4$ of $1$ and $3/2$, the perturbation adds $A$ and adds zero at both endpoints; since $A>D$, the midpoint log-convexity inequality is reversed.

items.title: FALSE: normalization and the functional equation determine the real Gamma function
items.strategy: Use the preceding periodic perturbation. It has the normalization and recurrence but differs from Gamma; its failure of log-convexity identifies the missing Bohr--Mollerup hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: Euler's real Gamma integral converges at the nonpositive integers
items.strategy: The convergence theorem says the Euler integral converges precisely for positive real parameters. At every nonpositive integer it diverges at zero. The later complex meromorphic continuation has poles there and is a different construction.

items.title: FALSE: unit-ball volume increases with dimension
items.strategy: The dimension-five maximum gives $V_6(1)<V_5(1)$ and the limit theorem gives $V_n(1)\to0$. Either fact refutes monotone increase; together they show the first failure and eventual behavior.
